records.why: The summary said the x direction is the left–right direction. In Aisha's mirror model the x direction is the one towards the mirror (her front-to-back direction), and a mirror reverses only that direction. Left and right only look swapped because the image faces her. Checked with her at x = 3 facing the wall: a hand raised at a given y stays at that y in the image, so the image has not moved the hand sideways; it has turned the whole body around.
records.old: standing at x = 3 in front of her mirror wall (the y-axis, x = 0), her image is located at x = −3, so the left–right (x) direction is flipped while the up–down (y) direction is preserved — which is exactly why the image raises the opposite hand.
records.new: standing at x = 3 in front of her mirror wall (the y-axis, x = 0), her image is located at x = −3. Only the x-coordinate, the direction towards the mirror, changes sign; the y-coordinate (her sideways and up–down position) stays the same. The raised hand stays at the same sideways position, but the image faces the opposite way, so it is the image's left hand. That is why it looks like the opposite hand.
records.group_headline: The explanation of the "flip" was wrong in several places: a mirror reverses only the direction towards the mirror (front to back); left and right only look swapped because the image faces us
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics, Chapter 25 Geometric Optics (plane mirrors and spherical mirrors); also the standard treatment of reflection as a reversal of the coordinate perpendicular to the mirror (e.g. Cambridge IGCSE/KICD Grade 10 Mathematics treatment of reflection)

records.why: Two corrections in one field: the flip explanation (same fix as the root item) and the claim that the matatu mirror shows vehicles at "their true apparent distance", which is not true for the convex side mirrors many matatus use (see the convex-mirror group).
records.old: Aisha's reflection raises the opposite hand because reflection reverses lateral orientation across the mirror line — a geometric consequence of the perpendicular-bisector rule. Her image appears exactly as far behind the mirror as she stands in front because the mirror line is equidistant from object and image. The matatu driver's rear-view mirror shows vehicles at their true apparent distance for the same reason.
records.new: Aisha's reflection appears to raise the opposite hand because reflection reverses only the direction towards the mirror, so the image faces her — a geometric consequence of the perpendicular-bisector rule. Her image appears exactly as far behind the mirror as she stands in front because the mirror line is equidistant from object and image. A flat rear-view mirror follows the same rules; curved convex mirrors follow them only approximately.
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics, Chapter 25 Geometric Optics (plane mirrors and spherical mirrors)

records.old: studies a diagram of a matatu side mirror and a diagram of a Kenyan road intersection with a convex safety mirror on a blind corner, then sketches the object (vehicle behind), the mirror line, and the image, and annotates which property explains why the image appears the same distance behind the mirror surface.

They sketch the object (vehicle behind), the mirror line and the image for the flat mirror only, and annotate which property explains why the image appears as far behind the mirror surface as the vehicle is in front of it. They then note one limit of the model: a curved convex mirror does not follow the three properties exactly (its image is smaller and sits closer to the mirror than the object is in front of it, but it shows a wider view).

records.why: In a flat mirror the driver sees the image of the hazard, so the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the hazard and its image, not of the driver and the hazard (with the old setup, the hazard's image would land on the driver's eye and the driver would see nothing useful). The same numbers are kept, only the labels change: H(−5, 3), I(1, 3). Checked: the midpoint of H and I is (−2, 3) and HI is horizontal, so the mirror line is x = −2; reflecting H(−5, 3) in x = −2 gives x = 2(−2) − (−5) = 1, so (1, 3) = I.
records.old: showing: a driver's eye position D(1, 3) and a road hazard H(-5, 3) on a Cartesian grid. They must find the equation of the mirror line that would allow the driver to see the hazard in a junction mirror — i.e., find the perpendicular bisector of DH.

records.why: The old argument was muddled (it claimed the distances become "smaller") and leaned on property 2 as an assumption. The new argument uses only the construction of the image: for a slanted line the perpendicular from P is a different line from PP′, so the image cannot land on P′. Checked with an example: P(0, 0), P′(2, 0), slanted line y = x − 1 through M(1, 0); the image of P in that line is (1, −1), not (2, 0).
records.old: Suppose a line through the midpoint is not perpendicular to PP′. Then the perpendicular distances from P and P′ to that line are smaller than the distance from each point to the midpoint, and the segment PP′ is not perpendicular to the line. That line would break property 2, so reflecting P in it would give a different image from P′. Only the perpendicular bisector makes P′ the true reflection of P.
records.new: Now suppose a line ℓ passes through the midpoint M of PP′ but is not perpendicular to PP′. To reflect P in ℓ, drop the perpendicular from P to ℓ and go the same distance beyond ℓ (as in Lesson 3). That perpendicular is a different line from PP′, so the image lies off the line PP′ and cannot be P′. Only the perpendicular bisector makes P′ the true reflection of P. In other words, the mirror line is exactly the set of points that are the same distance from P and from P′.
records.group_headline: Final Explanation 4(b) exemplar gave a muddled and circular reason why the mirror line must be the perpendicular bisector; replaced by a clear argument
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, "Perpendicular Bisector"; Euclid, Elements Book I (the perpendicular bisector of a segment is the set of points equidistant from its ends)
records.where: Final Explanation, Part 4: Finding a hidden mirror line, exemplar

records.why: The old sentence said another line would give a "non-congruent image". Every reflection gives a congruent image; the real problem is that the image lands in the wrong place. Checked with the example in the root record.

records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, "Perpendicular Bisector"; Euclid, Elements Book I (the perpendicular bisector of a segment is the set of points equidistant from its ends)

records.why: The old exemplar reused (x₁, y₁) for both point P and the midpoint, and mixed the general method with the special cases (the gradient formula fails when PP′ is vertical, because x₂ − x₁ = 0, and gives a negative reciprocal that does not exist when PP′ is horizontal, because m = 0). The midpoint now has its own symbols, the special cases come first, and a worked example is added. Checked the example: reflecting P(1, 2) in 2x + y − 9 = 0 gives (1, 2) + 2 × (2, 1) = (5, 4) = P′.
records.old: Step 1: find the midpoint of P(x₁, y₁) and P′(x₂, y₂) as ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Step 2: find the gradient m of PP′ as (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Step 3: the mirror line is perpendicular to PP′, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal, −1/m. Step 4: write the equation using y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), with the midpoint as the point (x₁, y₁) and −1/m as the gradient. Special cases: if PP′ is horizontal, the mirror line is vertical, x = the x-coordinate of the midpoint. If PP′ is vertical, the mirror line is horizontal, y = the y-coordinate of the midpoint.
records.new: Step 1: find the midpoint M of P(x₁, y₁) and P′(x₂, y₂): M = (xₘ, yₘ) = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). First check the special cases. If PP′ is horizontal (y₁ = y₂), the mirror line is vertical: x = xₘ. If PP′ is vertical (x₁ = x₂), the mirror line is horizontal: y = yₘ. Otherwise, Step 2: find the gradient m of PP′ as (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Step 3: the mirror line is perpendicular to PP′, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal, −1/m. Step 4: write the equation using y − yₘ = (−1/m)(x − xₘ), which passes through the midpoint. Example: P(1, 2) and P′(5, 4) give M = (3, 3) and m = 1/2, so the mirror gradient is −2 and y − 3 = −2(x − 3), that is y = −2x + 9.
records.group_headline: Final Explanation 4(c) exemplar reused the same symbols for P and the midpoint and did not separate the horizontal/vertical cases from the gradient method; rewritten with a worked example

value.criterion: Understanding of lines of symmetry and mirror lines
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: defines a line of symmetry accurately, links it to the mirror line, gives all correct counts for the shapes and explains why the fold and mirror tests agree.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: defines a line of symmetry and gives most counts correctly, with a partial link to the mirror line.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives an incomplete definition or several incorrect counts, with no link between folding and mirroring.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: states all three properties precisely, calculates 2.4 m correctly and uses the properties to explain the phenomenon fully, including why the image is the same size and directly across the mirror.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: states the three properties and calculates the distance correctly, with a partial explanation of the phenomenon.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: names fewer than three properties or makes errors in the distance calculation.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: gives all three rules correctly, finds all three images correctly and explains the flip correctly (only the x-coordinate, the direction towards the mirror, changes sign, so the image faces the opposite way).
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: gives the rules and most images correctly, with a limited explanation of the flip.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: confuses the rules or gives incorrect image coordinates.

value.criterion: Finding the mirror line and reasoning
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: describes the compass construction accurately, justifies the perpendicular bisector (a slanted line through the midpoint puts the image off the line PP′) and gives the full algebraic method with the horizontal and vertical special cases.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: describes the construction and gives a partial justification or most steps of the algebraic method.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives an unclear construction and no justification, or omits the perpendicular gradient.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: gives a coherent, accurate explanation that links the perpendicular bisector to all three properties, explains why the image appears reversed (it faces the object), refers to the matatu mirror and gives a Kenyan application.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: gives an accurate explanation that covers most ideas with some contexts.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives an explanation that is incomplete or has misconceptions, with few links to the phenomenon.

Below Expectations cannot be represented in the current contract. Suggested: teachers add the Below Expectations descriptor on the printed rubric by hand, or the partner contract is extended with a fourth level.

KICD wording check. No KICD source for Grade 10 Essential Mathematics is available in this workspace. The KICD Mathematics PDF (data/raw/curriculum_pdfs/Grade10_Mathematics_Curriculum.pdf) is the Core Mathematics design, where sub-strand 2.2 is called "Reflection and Congruence" (12 lessons), so KICD wording was NOT restored from it. Differences from the Core text that look worth a check against the Essential Mathematics design: (1) sub-strand title ("Reflection" here vs "Reflection and Congruence"); (2) 8 lessons here vs 12; (3) one key inquiry question here vs two in Core; (4) outcome (g), "appreciate the role of reflection in real-life situations", and the lines-of-symmetry content have no equivalent in the Core text beyond outcome (a); (5) the Lesson 8 reflection mentions the next sub-strand as "2.3 Trigonometry", whereas Core 2.3 is Rotation. Teachers should compare UNIT.learningOutcomes, content, key inquiry question, competencies, values and PCIs with the Essential Mathematics design.
